titleEn: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind
author: Yuval Noah Harari
introFa: کتاب «Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind» نوشته Yuval Noah Harari یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

Reviewed by RUSSELL TUTTLE University of Chicago Locomotion, like virtually all other be- haviors, should be seen in order to be fully comprehended. Yet remarkably few films on pongid locomotion are available despite the long recognized importance of knowledge about suspensory, climbing, and facultative bipedal postures and movements in apes for modeling hominoid phylogeny. Captive con- ditions are rarely appropriate to elicit an accurate representation of locomotion in free-ranging apes though anatomical potentialities for certain movements may be illustrated by proper stimulation or mani- pulation of captives. Most field studies and the films that are produced with them generally focus on social behavior to the extent that locomotion and other sub- sistence behaviors are slighted. The films reviewed here hardly begin to fill the need for representative illustrations of great ape and human locomotion. How- ever, they may be profitably employed in introductory and advanced evolutionary anthropology courses in which problems related to knuckle-walking and bipedal locomotion are considered. They should be augmented by visits to zoological gardens and studied observations of human as- sociates. E43, E44, and E45 show lateral, frontal, and posterior views of juvenile chimpanzee, gorilla, and orangutan subjects as they move quadrupedally atop a low level wall of masonry. Each film has sequences at 24 and 72 fps ("B/S") and contains close-up shots of hands and feet. The gaits shown in these films are summarized and discussed by Hildebrand (1967). The orangutan con- sistently fist-walks with fingers tightly flexed. This is a common hand posture in captive orangutans but it is only one of a wide variety of positions that are exhibited by individuals of the species (Tuttle 1967; Tuttle and Beck 1972; Tuttle and Basmajian All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

AUDIOVISUALS REVIEWS 2017 1973). The heel and lateral aspect of the sole are the major pressure points of the oran- gutan's feet. Its toes are flexed and its halluces touch the substratum. Again this is only one of a variety of postures exhibited by orangutans on the ground. Often their feet are markedly everted (cf. supinated) so that the halluces, medial toes and medial surface of the heels do not contact the ground. The pattern of knuckle-walking and the plantigrade foot postures of the chimpanzee and gorilla nicely exemplify those of juvenile African apes. Both subjects place their hands obliquely to the line of progression while many adult gorillas and some adult chim- panzees place their hands perpendicularly. E7 shows an adult female chimpanzee walking and galloping on a pathway and in the short grass beside it. She sometimes holds her left index finger free of the substrate without impairment of gait. The film is a good representation of adult chimpanzee knuckle-walking. E8 illustrates bipedal locomotion and vigilant stance in a chimpanzee. The subject runs on a pathway and on a wall. She leans forward and consistently exhibits a flexed knee, flexed thigh posture. Her feet are plantigrade as they are when she moves quadrupedally. There is no indication of a hominid sort of pelvic tilt mechanism. Instead she waddles. The films of human infants are of a very limited value for evolutionary anthropologi- cal studies even if one could compare them with similar films on infant apes. In E38 and E39 a nurse assists chubby babies, who are often shown only from the waist down, to walk across a padded surface. E76 shows an infant crawling a short distance on its palmigrade hands and knees across a padded surface. In E77 a prone baby (with ventrum on the mat) pulls himself forward with his elbows and pushes forward with his knees; his feet are upraised. In E84 a supine baby raises her head. Then a nurse pulls on her hands as she sits up. Finally the child flops forward so that her ventrum rests on her extended lower limbs. In E85 an infant hauls himself from a prone to an upright bipedal posture by gripping the vertical bars of his crib. To conclude, it would be more practical to have the best of the pongid locomotive sequences edited into a single six to ten minute film, with optional English sound track or printed guide sheet for those who do not understand German. The films of Homo sapiens may be left in their cannisters without detriment to the curriculum. References Cited Hildebrand, M. 1967 Symmetrical Gaits of Primates. Museum of Comparative Zoology Harvard University The title implies a broader, more com- parative coverage than is actually presented. The subjects-spider monkeys (Ateles) and baboons (Papio)-were filmed principally in outdoor runs in the Frankfort Zoo. The first half features spider monkeys in quadrupedal activity on flat ground, and displays well their habit of body posturing diagonal to their direction of progression. Bipedal walk- ing on chains suspended between trees emphasizes the agility and extraordinary sense of balance of these animals during bipedal activity.
